claims.text: Machine-learning potentials trained on ab initio DFT data can reproduce the melting temperature of refractory materials.
Machine-learning potentials trained on ab initio DFT data can reproduce the entropy of fusion of refractory materials.
Machine-learning potentials trained on ab initio DFT data can reproduce the enthalpy of fusion of refractory materials.
Machine-learning potentials trained on ab initio DFT data can reproduce the volume change at the melting point of refractory materials.
The accuracy of machine-learning-potential melting predictions is comparable to that of the full ab initio free-energy method.
Machine-learning-potential simulations have greatly reduced computational cost relative to direct ab initio free-energy calculations.
The reduced computational cost of machine-learning potentials makes high-throughput screening of refractory materials feasible.
Molecular dynamics driven by machine-learning potentials can replace ab initio molecular-dynamics thermodynamic integration for calculating melting properties.
The free-energy difference between solid and liquid phases mediates the melting transition.
The solid-liquid free-energy difference determines melting characteristics.
A machine-learning potential calibrated against DFT can approximate DFT interatomic interactions with high fidelity.
The computational efficiency and fidelity of the machine-learning potential allow simulations to capture anharmonic effects relevant to melting.
Machine-learning-potential simulations can capture solid-liquid phase coexistence needed to extract melting properties.
Melting properties can be extracted with machine-learning potentials using thermodynamic integration or two-phase coexistence methods without the computational cost of direct ab initio simulations.
Machine-learning potentials may require extensive training for each alloy system.
The accuracy of the proposed approach has not been tested across all classes of refractory materials.
Extrapolating a machine-learning potential to extreme thermodynamic conditions may introduce additional errors.
